messages.subject: Berkson measurement error model with inla.stack and multiple effects blocks
parts:
Hello,

I am trying to run a model that includes an SPDE model, fixed effects, and a (heteroscedastic) Berkson error model. I am using separate effects blocks in inla.stack for the SPDE model and the rest [i.e. stack = inla.stack( ... A=list(A.est, 1) ... ) ].

The NAs in stack$effects$data$w seem to cause an error for the meb model, as the values are not unique.

A minimal example (using a fixed effect for z, in place of the SPDE model):

#######################################################################
n <- 10
w <- 20 + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
s <- c(rep(2, n/2), rep(3, n/2))
z <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
y <- 10 + z + 3*(w + rnorm(n, 0, 1)) + rnorm(n, 0, 1)

stack <- inla.stack(data    = list(y = y),
                    A       = list(1, 1),
                    effects = list(list(z = z, intercept = 1),
                                   list(w = w, s = s)),
                    tag     = "t")

result <- inla(y ~ -1 + intercept + z + f(w, model  = "meb", scale = s, values = w),
               control.predictor = list(A       = inla.stack.A(stack),
                                        link    = 1,
                                        compute = TRUE),
               data = inla.stack.data(stack))
#######################################################################


Gives the error:

Error in inla(y ~ -1 + intercept + z + f(w, model = "meb", scale = s,  : 
  The 'values' given in f(w,..., values=...) are not unique:
    length(values)=20 but length(unique(values))=11


Is there any workaround for this? Or should I be specifying the model in some other way?

Regards,
Neil

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Berkson measurement error model with inla.stack and multiple effects blocks
parts:
Hi,
I think you're getting bitten by the scoping rules for the formula:
f(w, ..., values=w) will use the same w vector in both places, but
what you need is for the first one to be what the stack provides, and
the values one to be your original w-vector. Use different names for
them, e.g.
list(ww = w, s = s)
in the stack and
f(ww, ..., values=w)
in the formula.

Finn

Thank you for your reply.

Using list(ww = w, s = s) in the stack and  f(ww, ..., values=w) in the formula gives the error:
Error: length(random.spec$values) == ns is not TRUE

But using list(ww = w, ss = s) in the stack and  f(ww, ..., scale=s, values=w) in the formula, there is no error. Though the results are slightly different from what is produced when I use a stack with one effects block, or avoid using stack at all, with the following code.

## using 1 effects block -------------------------------------------------------
stack2 <- inla.stack(data    = list(y=y),
                     A       = list(1),
                     effects = list(list(z=z, intercept=1, w=w, s=s)),
                     tag     = "t")

result2 <- inla(y ~ -1 + intercept + z + f(w, model  = "meb", scale = s, values = w),
               control.predictor = list(A       = inla.stack.A(stack2),

link    = 1,
                                        compute = TRUE),

data = inla.stack.data(stack2))

## not  using stack ------------------------------------------------------------
adataframe <- data.frame(y         = inla.stack.data(stack2)$y,
                         intercept = inla.stack.data(stack2)$intercept,
                         z         = inla.stack.data(stack2)$z,
                         w         = inla.stack.data(stack2)$w,
                         s         = inla.stack.data(stack2)$s)

result3 <- inla(y ~ -1 + intercept + z + f(w, model  = "meb", scale = s, values = w),
               control.predictor = list(link    = 1,
                                        compute = TRUE),
               data = adataframe)

As an aside, I am also not entirely sure why these two models produce slightly different results, using the same formula on the same data values?

Regards,
Neil

parts:
As far as I can tell, the only correct combination in the thread so
far is a slight modification of the following one, where w and s are
_not_ part of the stack, since they describe the model itself, and
_not_ information for each observation:

"using list(ww = w, ss = s) in the stack and f(ww, ..., scale=s,
values=w) in the formula, there is no error."

Just use
list(ww=w_for_each_observation)
in the stack, and
f(ww, scale=s, values=w)
where (w[k], s[k]) are pairs of w-values and their corresponding s-values.
These should _not_ be constructed with inla.stack.

At least that's what I take from the inla.doc("meb") text, for how to
construct a heteroscedastic model (the scale values seem to go into
the D matrix there, even though that's not explicitly spelled out).

Finn

Thank you. I can use that method.

I am concerned, though, that using the Berkson error model seems to give different results depending on the order of the data. For example, the following two INLA calls give different results:

n <- 100
w <- 20 + rnorm(n, 0, 1)

z <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
y <- 10 + z + 3*(w + rnorm(n, 0, 1)) + rnorm(n, 0, 1)

data <- data.frame(w=w, z=z, y=y, intercept=1)
data2 <- data[sample(1:nrow(data)),]

result <- inla(y ~ -1 + intercept + z + f(w, model  = "meb"),
               data = data)

result2 <- inla(y ~ -1 + intercept + z + f(w, model  = "meb"),
                data = data2)

result$summary.fixed
result2$summary.fixed
On Tuesday, May 8, 2018 at 1:27:53 PM UTC+1, Finn Lindgren wrote:

As far as I can tell, the only correct combination in the thread so
far is a slight modification of the following one, where w and s are
_not_ part of the stack, since they describe the model itself, and
_not_ information for each observation:

"using list(ww = w, ss = s) in the stack and  f(ww, ..., scale=s,
values=w) in the formula, there is no error."

Just use
  list(ww=w_for_each_observation)
in the stack, and
  f(ww, scale=s, values=w)
where (w[k], s[k]) are pairs of w-values and their corresponding s-values.
These should _not_ be constructed with inla.stack.

At least that's what I take from the inla.doc("meb") text, for how to
construct a heteroscedastic model (the scale values seem to go into
the D matrix there, even though that's not explicitly spelled out).

Finn
